div.head: Chapter 9
div.p: The illustrious kings of Castile and León, after they offered and obligated themselves by their own solemn promise to take charge of ensuring that the Catholic faith be preached and those Indian peoples converted, are bound by divine precept to bear the costs and expenses that shall be necessary for the achievement of the said end, and they may not compel the Indians by any temporal or bodily penalty to pay those costs, nor any part of them, if the Indians of their own free will do not wish to pay them.

The first part is proved because every Catholic king is bound by divine precept to exalt, spread, and defend the Catholic faith and Christian religion at his own cost, not only of money, but, if it should be necessary, to risk and lose his very life for it; and especially if the vicar of Christ, the Supreme Pontiff, should command it by precept. The first point is proved because every faithful Christian is bound to confess the faith through outward acts, according to the matter and ability he has, as that passage of Romans 10 says: "For with the mouth confession is made unto salvation," and that of Mark 8 and Luke 9 and 12: "Whoever confesses me before men, him will I also confess before my Father. And whoever is ashamed of me, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, etc." That is to say, whenever a case arises in which the divine honor and glory would be diminished, or neighboring Christians would suffer some danger to their spiritual salvation: on this, Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 4 a. 1 et 2. Now kings are faithful Christians and the causes of the faith are common to every Christian, as appears in 96 dist., c. ubinam legistis, etc. et c. Nos ad fidem, 23, q. 5, c. "The princes of this world not infrequently hold within the Church the heights of power they have obtained, so that through that same power they may defend ecclesiastical discipline, etc. Let the princes of this world know that they must render account to God for the Church which they receive from Christ to protect, etc." Therefore faithful Christian kings and princes, with all their strength are bound by divine law to confess the faith, whether by exalting it, defending it, spreading it, or preserving it, which are the outward acts by which they manifest the faith held by all faithful Christians.

The second point is likewise proved, namely, and especially so, if the vicar of Christ, the Supreme Pontiff, commands it by precept; because the Supreme Pontiff may command any Christian king as a minister of the kingdom of Jesus Christ, according to that passage of Wisdom 6: "Hear, O kings of the earth, and understand; learn, you who are judges of the ends of the earth; for power was given to you by the Lord and strength by the Most High, because being ministers of his kingdom, etc."; et Romans 13; that at his own cost and expense, after having supplied the needs of his own kingdom, he supply and assist those of the universal Church, both to extend it and to defend and preserve it, and the king is bound by divine precept to obey him as he would Jesus Christ himself. This is evident because the pope is the supreme Architect, as the master builder of the entire spiritual edifice which he directs and leads toward the ultimate end of eternal life. It belongs to the office of the Architect, to whom the ultimate end pertains, to order and command the ministers who are to employ the means and subordinate ends directed toward the achievement of the ultimate end, as philosophy professes, ut in I Metaphysicorum; and to him everything must be subject insofar as this is fitting for the aforesaid purpose. Therefore, in matters of the faith and those concerning the spiritual edifice of the Christian religion, kings are subject to the vicar of Christ and bound to obey and fulfill his commandments as those of Jesus Christ himself, according to that passage of Luke 10: "He who hears you, hears me; and he who despises you, despises me"; and Saint Paul, Hebrews 13: "Obey your prelates, etc." And Saint Cyril in the Book of Treasures, after much else: "But that as members they may remain in our head, the apostolic throne of the Roman pontiffs, from whom we must inquire what we ought to believe and what to hold, venerating him, beseeching him before all others, for it belongs to him alone to rebuke, correct, and establish, and dispose, and loose, and in his place to bind the one whom he has built up; and to no other but to him alone did he give what is his. To whom all by divine right bow their heads, and the princes of the world obey as Christ the Lord Jesus, etc."; and Saint Thomas, De regimine principum, lib. 1, cap. 24, says the same, and in lib. 2 Sentent., dist. 44, in fin., and on the Epistle 2 Corinthians, cap. 12, lectio 2, and Philippians, cap. 4, he says that to provide for the needs of one land, the pope may impose a subsidy upon other parts of the world. In keeping with what has been said, what the pope recalls in the bull of concession of the Indies, where he adjures and conjures the kings of Castile and León: "by the reception of the holy baptism," he says, "by which you are bound to the apostolic commandments, etc.," and thus he imposed a formal precept upon them, binding them to what was said. "And furthermore," he says, "we command you in virtue of holy obedience, as you also promise, and we do not doubt that you will carry out by your very great devotion and royal magnanimity, that you must dispatch to the said mainland and islands men who are upright and God-fearing, learned and skilled, to instruct the said inhabitants and dwellers in the Catholic faith and imbue them with good morals, applying to all of this every due diligence, etc." And so it appears that the pope was able to bind, and did bind, the lords kings of Castile and León to the preaching of the faith and the conversion of those peoples, and consequently to the expenses necessary to achieve that end. And the reason is clear because, once the precept of the end has been imposed, it necessarily follows that a precept has been imposed for the means without which the end cannot be achieved, ex 2 Physicorum and Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 44 a. 1, and it is a matter for jurists in cap. 1 y cap. preterea, De officio delegati. The means necessary for this are the expenses, and especially since the said lords kings offered themselves to this, and by their own solemn promise bound themselves to it, as appears from the words of the bull cited above. The first part of the principle is therefore proved.
